title: Prefix, Root and Suffix
short: Most long words are built from parts: a prefix in front, a root in the middle and a suffix at the end.
trouble: Learners split words by spelling alone (seeing "pen" in "repent") or assume every word with a familiar part carries its meaning. A root is a clue to check against the sentence, not a guarantee.

blocks.html: A long word can look like a wall of letters. Look again and you will often find it is built from parts, like train cars hooked together. Take unbreakable: un- (not) + break + -able (able to be). Put the parts together and the meaning falls out: “not able to be broken.”

blocks.name: vo-scene

scene.alt: A girl points at three boxes labeled UN, BREAK and ABLE: a prefix, a root and a suffix.

blocks.cap: A girl points at three boxes labeled UN, BREAK and ABLE: a prefix, a root and a suffix.

blocks.html: A prefix goes at the front and changes the meaning (un-, re-, pre-). The root is the core that carries the main idea (break, cred, spect). A suffix goes at the end and usually tells you the part of speech (-able and -ous make adjectives; -tion makes nouns; -ize makes verbs).

Many roots are not English words on their own. cred (believe) and spect (look) came from Latin, so you meet them only inside words: credible, incredulous, inspect, spectator. Once you know a root, every word built on it gets easier. Here is one root, port (carry), with its family:

blocks.title: Take a word apart
blocks.q: What does transportable mean? Take it apart first.
steps: Find the prefix at the front: trans-, which means “across.”
Find the suffix at the end: -able, which means “able to be.”
What is left is the root: port, “carry.”
Put the parts together: “able to be carried across.”
Check it in a sentence: “The stage was built in pieces, so it was easy to load on a truck; it was transportable.” The meaning fits.
blocks.a: Able to be moved from one place to another.

blocks.name: vo-word

entry.def: unwilling or unable to believe something
entry.ex: Maya gave an {incredulous} laugh when her little brother said he had cleaned his room.
entry.ctx: When the waiter announced that their meal was free, the diners were {incredulous}; they asked him three times whether he was joking.
entry.note: A story can be incredible (hard to believe); the person hearing it is incredulous (not believing).

mn.text: Kai says he cleaned his room, but Maya can see socks on the floor and books on the bed. Her raised eyebrows are {incredulous}.

scene.alt: A boy claims his messy room is clean while his sister stares in disbelief.

blocks.cap: A word from the list: incredulous.

blocks.html: Splitting a word by its letters alone. The pen in repent is not a writing pen, and uncle does not start with un-: these letters only look like parts. A part is a clue, not a guarantee. Use it to make a guess, then check the guess against the sentence the word is in.

A good habit for any new word: (1) look for a prefix, (2) look for a suffix, (3) see what root is left, (4) put the meanings together, and (5) test your guess in the sentence. The rest of this course teaches the parts that show up most often in strong writing.
